dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision a container using Azure Container Instances
domanda: A nightly image-rendering job runs as a single Linux container in Azure Container Instances. The job runs a script that exits when the rendering completes. You must ensure that the container is not restarted after the script completes successfully, but that it is restarted automatically if the script terminates with a nonzero exit code. Which restart policy should you configure for the container group?
spiegazione: OnFailure restarts the containers in the group only when the process executed in the container fails, that is, when it terminates with a nonzero exit code. The containers therefore run at least once, and a successful exit leaves the container in the Terminated state, which is exactly the required behavior. Always is incorrect: it is the default policy applied when no restart policy is specified, and it restarts the containers unconditionally, so the container would be restarted even after a successful run. Never is incorrect: the containers run at most once and are never restarted, so a failed rendering script would not be retried. UnlessStopped is incorrect: it is a Docker restart policy value and is not one of the three restart policy settings supported by Azure Container Instances, which are Always, Never, and OnFailure.
tags: azure container instances,aci,restart policy,onfailure,container group,run-once task

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision a container using Azure Container Instances
domanda: A development team asks you to deploy a container group to Azure Container Instances that contains an application container and a logging sidecar container. Both containers are built from Windows Server base images. What should you tell the team?
opzione_a: The deployment is supported. Create the container group with the OS type set to Windows and define both containers in the containers array.
opzione_b: Multi-container groups support only Linux containers. For Windows containers, Azure Container Instances supports the deployment of a single container instance only.
opzione_c: The deployment is supported only if the container group is deployed into a delegated subnet of an Azure virtual network.
opzione_d: The deployment is supported only if the two containers are placed in separate container groups that communicate over localhost.
spiegazione: Multi-container groups in Azure Container Instances currently support only Linux containers. For Windows containers, Azure Container Instances supports the deployment of a single container instance only, so an application container plus a logging sidecar in one group requires Linux images. Option a is incorrect because setting the OS type to Windows does not lift the restriction; running multiple containers per container group is one of the features restricted to Linux. Option c is incorrect because virtual network deployment does not enable Windows multi-container groups; it is an unrelated networking capability. Option d is incorrect on two counts: splitting the containers into separate groups defeats the sidecar pattern, and localhost communication works only between container instances inside the same container group, never across groups.
tags: azure container instances,aci,container group,multi-container,windows containers,os type,sidecar

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision a container using Azure Container Instances
domanda: A Linux container group in Azure Container Instances mounts an Azure file share as a volume so that the application can persist log files. A security review requires that no storage account key appear in the container group definition. A colleague proposes assigning a user-assigned managed identity to the container group and using it to mount the file share. How should you respond?
opzione_a: Grant the managed identity the Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor role on the share, then remove the storage account key from the volume definition.
opzione_b: Azure Storage does not support SMB mounting of a file share by using a managed identity, so the storage account key is still required for the Azure Files volume.
opzione_c: Add a service endpoint for Azure Storage to the delegated subnet, which allows the mount to authenticate with the managed identity instead of a key.
opzione_d: Change the OS type of the container group to Windows, because managed identity authentication for Azure Files volumes is supported only for Windows containers.
spiegazione: The Azure Files volume documentation for Azure Container Instances states explicitly that Azure Storage does not support SMB mounting of a file share by using a managed identity. Mounting an Azure file share as a volume requires three values: the storage account name, the share name, and the storage account key. Option a is incorrect because the Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor role enables identity-based access for supported scenarios such as domain-joined clients, but it does not allow an Azure Container Instances volume mount to authenticate without the key. Option c is incorrect because a service endpoint to Azure Storage only provides network reachability when outbound internet access is blocked in the delegated subnet; it changes network path, not authentication. Option d is incorrect and reverses the actual limitation: Azure Files shares can only be mounted to Linux containers, and the mount requires the container to run as root.
tags: azure container instances,aci,volume mount,azure files,smb,managed identity,storage account key

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision a container using Azure Container Apps
domanda: A microservices solution runs in an Azure Container Apps environment named env1. A container app named web1 serves a web front end and must be reachable from the internet. A container app named orders1 exposes an HTTP API that must be callable only by other container apps in env1 and must not be reachable from the public internet. What should you configure for orders1?
opzione_b: Enable ingress for orders1 and set the ingress traffic type to Internal.
opzione_c: Enable ingress for orders1, set the ingress traffic type to External, and add IP restrictions that deny all public IP address ranges.
opzione_d: Enable ingress for orders1 and configure session affinity so that requests are pinned to replicas inside the environment.
spiegazione: Internal ingress makes an app reachable only from within the same Container Apps environment, such as from other container apps, and the app is not directly accessible from the public internet. That is precisely the requirement for orders1, while web1 keeps External ingress. Option a is incorrect because disabling ingress removes the app's endpoint entirely, so web1 would have no way to call the orders API over HTTP. Option c is incorrect because External ingress exposes the app through the environment's inbound IP address; relying on deny rules to undo that exposure is a fragile workaround, and the documented mechanism for environment-only reachability is Internal ingress. Option d is incorrect because session affinity (sticky sessions) only routes a client's HTTP requests to the same replica; it has no effect on whether the app is exposed publicly.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage sizing and scaling for containers, including Azure Container Instances and Azure Container Apps
domanda: A container app named worker1 pulls messages from an on-premises message broker over an outbound connection. Ingress is disabled for worker1, no scale rule is defined, and the minimum replica count is left at its default value. After deployment, worker1 processes messages for a short time and then stops processing permanently, and the revision shows a running status of Scale to 0. You must ensure that worker1 keeps processing messages. The solution must not enable ingress. What should you do?
opzione_a: Set the minimum number of replicas for the revision to 1.
opzione_b: Add an HTTP scale rule with the concurrent requests threshold set to 1.
opzione_c: Change the revision mode of worker1 from Single to Multiple.
opzione_d: Increase the maximum number of replicas for the revision from 10 to 30.
spiegazione: The default minimum replica count per revision is 0 and the default maximum is 10. Microsoft Learn warns that you must create a scale rule or set minReplicas to 1 or more if you do not enable ingress, because with ingress disabled and neither a minimum replica count nor a custom scale rule defined, the container app scales to zero and has no way of starting back up. Setting the minimum replicas to 1 guarantees that an instance of the revision is always running. Option b is incorrect because an HTTP scale rule scales on the number of concurrent HTTP requests to the revision; with ingress disabled, no inbound HTTP requests can reach worker1, so the rule can never trigger a scale-out from zero. Option c is incorrect because the revision mode only controls how many revisions can be active simultaneously and how traffic is split between them; it does not affect replica scaling. Option d is incorrect because the maximum replica count only caps scale-out; the app is stuck at zero replicas, and raising the ceiling never causes the first replica to be created.
tags: azure container apps,scaling,scale to zero,min replicas,keda,ingress disabled,troubleshooting

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision a container using Azure Container Apps
domanda: You manage a container app named api1 that runs in multiple revision mode. You need to identify which planned change will cause Azure Container Apps to create a new revision when the app is deployed. Which change creates a new revision?
opzione_a: Changing the traffic split weights between two active revisions
opzione_b: Updating the value of a secret that is referenced by the app
opzione_c: Updating the container image to a new tag
opzione_d: Turning off ingress for the app
spiegazione: A revision-scope change is any change to parameters in the properties.template section of the container app resource, which includes the revision suffix, container configuration and images, and scale rules. Updating the container image to a new tag is therefore a revision-scope change and triggers a new, immutable revision. The other three options are application-scope changes, defined as changes to parameters in the properties.configuration section; they are applied globally to all revisions and do not create a new revision. Option a is incorrect because traffic splitting rules are part of the ingress configuration. Option b is incorrect because secret values are application-scope; note that revisions must be restarted before a container recognizes new secret values, but no new revision is produced. Option d is incorrect because turning ingress on or off is part of the ingress configuration and is likewise application-scope.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision a container using Azure Container Instances
domanda: Your organization runs workloads in Azure Container Instances and is evaluating whether some of them can be migrated from Linux images to Windows images. You need to identify the capabilities that are currently restricted to Linux containers in Azure Container Instances. Which capabilities are restricted to Linux containers? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Mounting an Azure Files share as a volume in the container group
opzione_b: Running multiple containers in a single container group
opzione_c: Assigning a DNS name label to the container group so that it is reachable by FQDN
opzione_d: Collecting container resource usage metrics with Azure Monitor
opzione_e: Configuring a restart policy of OnFailure for the container group
spiegazione: The Azure Container Instances overview lists the features that are currently restricted to Linux containers: multiple containers per container group, volume mounting (Azure Files, emptyDir, GitRepo, and secret volumes), resource usage metrics with Azure Monitor, and GPU resources (preview). Options a, b, and d map directly to that list. Option c is incorrect because container access through an IP address and a DNS name label that produces an FQDN of the form dns-name-label.region.azurecontainer.io is available for container groups regardless of OS type. Option e is incorrect because the restart policy settings Always, Never, and OnFailure are properties of the container group and apply to both Linux and Windows deployments.
tags: azure container instances,aci,os type,linux containers,windows containers,volume mount,azure monitor metrics

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage sizing and scaling for containers, including Azure Container Instances and Azure Container Apps
domanda: While designing the autoscale configuration for a set of container apps, you need to identify the trigger types that Azure Container Apps supports for scale rules. Which triggers can you use? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: The number of concurrent HTTP requests to the revision
opzione_b: The number of concurrent TCP connections to the revision
opzione_c: The number of messages in an Azure Service Bus queue
opzione_d: The disk IOPS consumed by the replica's ephemeral storage
opzione_e: A vertical resize of the replica's CPU and memory when memory pressure exceeds a threshold
spiegazione: Azure Container Apps implements scaling with KEDA and supports three categories of triggers: HTTP, based on the number of concurrent HTTP requests to the revision; TCP, based on the number of concurrent TCP connections to the revision; and custom, based on custom metrics such as CPU and memory or supported event-driven data sources including Azure Service Bus, Azure Event Hubs, Apache Kafka, and Redis. Options a, b, and c match those categories, with the Service Bus queue length implemented as a custom KEDA scaler. Option d is incorrect because disk IOPS on ephemeral storage is not a documented Container Apps trigger category or supported event source. Option e is incorrect because it describes vertical scaling, which the scaling documentation lists explicitly as a known limitation: vertical scaling is not supported. Container Apps scales horizontally by adding and removing replicas.
tags: azure container apps,keda,scale rules,http scaling,tcp scaling,custom scaler,azure service bus,vertical scaling

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision a container using Azure Container Apps
domanda: A container app named catalog1 currently has a single active revision that serves production traffic. Your change management policy states that any deployment which creates a new revision requires a change record. You need to identify the changes that can be deployed to catalog1 WITHOUT creating a new revision. Which changes qualify? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Updating the value of a secret stored in the container app
opzione_b: Changing the revision mode from Single to Multiple
opzione_c: Updating the container image reference in the app's template
opzione_d: Adding a KEDA scale rule to the app
opzione_e: Turning off ingress for the app
spiegazione: Application-scope changes are changes to parameters in the properties.configuration section of the container app resource. They are applied globally to all revisions and do not create a new revision. The documented application-scope parameters include secret values, the revision mode, ingress configuration (turning ingress on or off, traffic splitting rules, and labels), credentials for private container registries, and Dapr settings. Options a, b, and e are therefore all application-scope. Options c and d are incorrect because they are revision-scope changes: a revision-scope change is any change to the parameters in the properties.template section, which explicitly includes the revision suffix, container configuration and images, and scale rules for the container application. Both would produce a new, immutable revision on deployment.

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision a container using Azure Container Instances
domanda: Contoso must run a nightly data-conversion task in Azure Container Instances. The task runs a script that writes its output files to a share so the files survive after the container stops, and the container must be restarted automatically only if the script exits with a nonzero exit code. During the run, an operator must be able to reach a status page hosted by the container by using a fully qualified domain name that is based on a DNS name label. Select the appropriate option for each setting.
opzione_a: OS type: [Linux | Windows | Windows Server Core]
opzione_c: Volume type to mount for the output files: [Azure Files | Azure Blob Storage | Azure NetApp Files]
opzione_d: FQDN suffix produced by the DNS name label: [.azurewebsites.net | .azurecontainer.io | .azurecontainerapps.io]
spiegazione: OS type must be Linux because volume mounting, including Azure Files shares, is one of the features restricted to Linux containers in Azure Container Instances. Restart policy must be OnFailure, because it restarts the containers only when the process executed in the container terminates with a nonzero exit code; Always would restart the container after a successful run, and Never would leave a failed run unretried. The volume type must be Azure Files: to persist state beyond the lifetime of the container, Azure Container Instances can mount an Azure file share created with Azure Files over SMB, and the supported volume types are Azure file share, secret, emptyDir, and cloned git repo. Azure Blob Storage and Azure NetApp Files are not supported volume types for a container group. The FQDN suffix is .azurecontainer.io, because a container instance with a DNS name label is publicly reachable at dns-name-label.region.azurecontainer.io; .azurewebsites.net belongs to Azure App Service and .azurecontainerapps.io belongs to Azure Container Apps environments.
tags: azure container instances,aci,hotspot,os type,restart policy,azure files,dns name label,fqdn

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Manage sizing and scaling for containers, including Azure Container Instances and Azure Container Apps
domanda: A junior administrator deploys a container app to a Container Apps environment and accepts every scale-related default, without defining any scale rule and without changing the replica limits. You must document the resulting scale configuration. Select the appropriate option for each setting.
opzione_a: Default minimum number of replicas per revision: [0 | 1 | 3]
opzione_b: Default maximum number of replicas per revision: [10 | 30 | 300]
opzione_c: Trigger used by the default scale rule: [HTTP | CPU | Azure Service Bus]
opzione_d: Default concurrent requests threshold for an HTTP scale rule: [1 | 10 | 100]
spiegazione: The Container Apps scale limits table gives a default of 0 for the minimum number of replicas per revision and a default of 10 for the maximum number of replicas per revision; the maximum value configurable for either limit is 1,000. When you do not create a scale rule, the documented default scale rule uses an HTTP trigger with min replicas 0 and max replicas 10, which is why HTTP is correct rather than CPU or Azure Service Bus (both of those are available only as custom KEDA rules that you must define yourself). The concurrentRequests property of an HTTP scale rule has a default value of 10 and a minimum value of 1: when the number of concurrent HTTP requests exceeds this value, the app adds another replica, up to maxReplicas.
tags: azure container apps,scaling,defaults,min replicas,max replicas,http scale rule,concurrent requests,keda

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision a container using Azure Container Apps
domanda:
A container app named api1 runs in a Container Apps environment named env1. The app is configured with ingress enabled and set to External, HTTP transport, a target port of 8080, a minimum replica count of 0, a maximum replica count of 10, and the default Single revision mode. No custom scale rule is defined. Evaluate each of the following statements about api1. For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

1. Clients on the internet can reach api1 over HTTPS on port 443 by using the app's fully qualified domain name.
2. If api1 stops receiving requests, it can scale in to zero replicas, and you incur no usage charges while it is scaled to zero.
3. You can split incoming traffic between two revisions of api1 without changing the current revision mode.
opzione_a: Clients on the internet can reach api1 over HTTPS on port 443 by using the app's fully qualified domain name.
opzione_b: If api1 stops receiving requests, it can scale in to zero replicas, and you incur no usage charges while it is scaled to zero.
opzione_c: You can split incoming traffic between two revisions of api1 without changing the current revision mode.
spiegazione: Statement 1 is Yes: with HTTP ingress enabled, a container app exposes ports 80 for HTTP and 443 for HTTPS, receives a fully qualified domain name based on the environment's DNS suffix, and terminates TLS at the ingress point; because ingress is External, the app is exposed through the environment's inbound IP address and can receive traffic from the public internet. The target port of 8080 is the port the container listens on internally and does not change the externally exposed ports. Statement 2 is Yes: the minimum replica count is 0, and the scaling documentation states that you are not billed usage charges if your container app scales to zero. Statement 3 is No: traffic splitting between active revisions requires multiple revision mode. By default, when ingress is enabled, all traffic is routed to the latest deployed revision, and you can split incoming traffic between active revisions only when you enable multiple revision mode; api1 is currently in Single revision mode, so the mode must be changed first.
tags: azure container apps,ingress,external,https,scale to zero,billing,revision mode,traffic splitting

dominio: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
sotto_argomento: Provision a container using Azure Container Apps
domanda: A container app named album-api has a single active revision that serves 100 percent of the traffic. You plan to release an updated container image and gradually phase it in by sending 20 percent of the incoming traffic to the new version while the current version keeps serving the remaining 80 percent. You must perform the release from the Azure portal. Which four actions should you perform in sequence? Arrange the actions in the correct order.
opzione_a: Enter the percentage of traffic to route to each revision so that the combined percentage equals 100 percent, and then select Save.
opzione_b: Open the album-api container app and select Revision management.
opzione_c: Select Create new revision, specify a name suffix and the updated container image, and then select Create.
opzione_d: Select Choose revision mode, select Multiple: Several revisions active simultaneously, and then select Apply.
spiegazione: The documented portal procedure for traffic splitting is: first open the container app and select Revision management, which is the blade where revision mode, revision creation, and traffic weights are managed. Next, because the app is in Single revision mode, select Choose revision mode, select Multiple: Several revisions active simultaneously, and select Apply, then wait for the revision mode to update to Multiple; multiple revision mode is a prerequisite because traffic can only be split between active revisions when that mode is enabled. Then create the new revision by selecting Create new revision, entering a name suffix, and specifying the updated image; this is a revision-scope change that produces a second revision. Finally, mark the revisions as Active and enter the traffic percentage for each revision in the Traffic column, ensuring the combined percentage of all traffic equals 100 percent, and select Save. Setting the weights before a second revision exists would leave nothing to split traffic to, so the weight step must come last.
tags: azure container apps,traffic splitting,revisions,multiple revision mode,azure portal,blue-green,drag drop
